# A fence must gate every write, not merely appear in it

<!-- review-bot-scope:start -->
packages/store-*/src/**/*.ts
packages/core/src/fenced-batch.ts
packages/core/src/sql-tree.ts
packages/core/src/statements/**/*.ts
<!-- review-bot-scope:end -->

Scope: `packages/store-*/src/**/*.ts` and `packages/core/src/fenced-batch.ts` — the SQL of every dialect store and the primitive that builds it. The question this rule asks of a diff is WHICH ROWS a statement may write and what proves this batch produced them. Deliberately not covered here: which instant a statement may read (§3.4 rule 8b, the clock-in-a-follow-on class — a sibling rule owns `$NOW$`, `fence_at_ms` and the one-instant-per-batch property); validation of client numbers at the port (rule 7); terminal-task inertness as a policy question (rule 6) except where a `narrow` guard is the thing being weakened; and the postmortem/attestation gate. Reads are in scope only through `openTail`.

Every store operation is one atomic batch. Later statements see earlier statements' effects, so a statement's own WHERE cannot tell "my compare-and-set won" from "the row already looked like this". DESIGN.md §3.4 rule 1 says a follow-on keys on the post-transition state PLUS this batch's stamp; rule 8 says the stamp lives in `fence_stamp`/`fence_at_ms` and names a STATEMENT (`<seed>:<name>`), never a batch. This is the recurring class in this repo's history: fourteen of the forty-four findings in `postmortems/pr3.6-fence-provenance.md`, in review rounds 1, 3, 5 and 6, after round 1 had already instituted a rung-1 mechanism against it — and finding 39 was the class occurring INSIDE the generator built to end it.

What it costs when it ships, from that postmortem: a duplicate activation that correctly LOST its compare-and-set still matched the task follow-on (which was fenced on `claimed_by` and `activated_gen` — values the winner wrote and any second delivery sees identically) and cleared the task's armed cancellation deadline, so a task that was never started is now never cancelled. `emitEvent` read task ids off `waits` instead of off the runs it woke, so a corrupt wait row naming an unrelated healthy task flipped that task to pending while its own run kept running. `awaitEvent`'s park took `available_at_ms` from any waiting row for the event, so a 30-second await inherited a stale row's NULL timeout and parked the run forever. A wake predicate split into an index driver and a witness let two DIFFERENT wait rows — each individually disqualifying — answer one condition apiece, and the run woke on a registration that did not exist. None of these throw, none log, and every later read looks ordinary. Note the failure in the other direction too: a fenced statement that can never match anything (`key: 'run_id'` against `column: 'task_id'`) is silent forever, and a follow-on that never runs looks exactly like one with nothing to do.

<!-- review-bot-synopsis:start -->
Flag a non-CAS statement that can write rows it did not prove this batch produced: no top-level `fence_stamp = fence(...)` conjunct, a fence past a top-level OR or under NOT, a hand-written UPDATE/DELETE `followOn` where `derived()` should generate the selection, a follow-on keyed on post-state a duplicate delivery leaves identical (or on the pre-condition the CAS consumed), a stamp-fenced INSERT with no ownership replay guard (or a diff deleting one), a `derived()` `key`/`column` pair naming different identifier kinds, a follow-on selecting from a table the batch never wrote (or a condition added to `wake-runs`'s `IN` driver without its `EXISTS` witness), a value or identifier read from a row no fence of this batch gates, a stamp used as proof of authorship, a multi-statement `db.batch` write with no structural fence of its own, or caller text spliced unbracketed into a boolean position in `fenced-batch.ts`. Pass for `openTail` reads fenced on a lease token or unique index (`picked`, `receipt`, `hit`), CAS guards over unwritten tables and CAS counter bumps, `fragments.ts`'s ownership predicates, `checkpointWrite`'s attempt tiebreak, shrink-only `narrow:` clauses (including the `f` alias inside their own subqueries), bracketed ORs from `cancelNotDue`/`eligibleTask` and inside a `derived()` `where:`, post-state in a `derived()` `where:`, generated provenance on `derived()` updates, `wake-runs` itself, `heartbeat`/`expireLeaseNow`/`driverHeartbeat`, read-mode batches, and `admin.ts`'s sentinel-fenced migration batches.
<!-- review-bot-synopsis:end -->

Report a failure when the changed code introduces, or materially widens, any of these:

- **A writing statement with no positive fence dominating it.** For any statement that is not a compare-and-set: no `fence_stamp = <a fence of this batch>` as a top-level AND conjunct of the WHERE side. The fence appears only in the SET clause, only inside a scalar subquery that feeds SET, only inside a comment, or only under `NOT (...)` / `NOT EXISTS (...)`. A statement asserting the fence is ABSENT is not a fenced statement. `FencedBatch` throws on this shape at construction, so the live instances are raw `db.batch` writes and any new dialect's own SQL.
- **A fence that is present and gates nothing.** A top-level `OR` in the WHERE of a follow-on or tail, so the fence can be false while the row is still written; or a `derived()` `narrow:` that introduces an alternation weakening a target-side guard. `WHERE run_id = ? OR EXISTS (… fence …)` is the exact recorded false negative — present, positive, in the WHERE, and reaching nothing. A CAS is exempt: its guard consumes the pre-state and is its own proof, so alternative pre-conditions are legitimate there.
- **A caller-authored WHERE where `derived()` should generate the selection.** A `followOn` whose SQL is an UPDATE or a DELETE. `emitEvent`'s `wake-runs` is the only one in the tree; every other UPDATE/DELETE follow-on is generated, and the primitive builds `key IN (SELECT f.<column> FROM <from> f WHERE (<where>) AND f.fence_stamp = …)` and ANDs `narrow`, so it can only shrink. A second hand-written one re-opens the surface for every future reader, not just this diff.
- **Proof taken from the post-state, or from the pre-condition the CAS just consumed.** A hand-written follow-on keyed on values the winning statement WROTE that a previous delivery of the same request leaves identical (`claimed_by = ?`, `activated_gen = ?`, `state = 'running'`) with no fence conjunct beside them; or a `derived()` `where:` naming the state the CAS CONSUMED rather than the one it wrote (`where: f.state = 'pending'` after the CAS set `'running'`), which is fenced, generated, and matches nothing forever.
- **A stamp-fenced INSERT with no ownership guard against its own replay.** An exact re-delivery of the same compiled batch re-binds the same seed, so `f.fence_stamp = ${b.fence('x')}` still matches the row the first delivery stamped and the INSERT fires again — dying on a primary key or unique index and discarding a whole tick, or worse, committing a half-transition. Every successor INSERT and terminal arm asks `successorOwned(id, task, intendedAttempt)` whether that exact immutable successor already exists; spawn uses `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM runs r WHERE r.task_id = f.task_id)`. Flag a new INSERT without an ownership guard, and flag any diff that deletes or weakens an existing one.
- **A `derived()` spec whose two identifier sides do not match.** `key` names a column of `target` and `column` names a column of `from`; if they are different kinds of identifier the statement compiles, is fenced, is generated — and matches nothing, ever.
- **A follow-on selecting its row set from a table this batch never wrote.** `emitEvent`'s `wake-runs` is the single documented escape (§3.4 rule 2). Adding another, or widening this one, is the finding: a condition added to the `IN (SELECT w.run_id FROM waits w …)` index driver without the same condition on the `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM waits s …)` witness (or the reverse), removal of `s.queue = runs.queue`, or a cleanup/delete keyed on the event name rather than derived from the runs `wake-runs` stamped — that last one deletes registrations of runs it declined to wake, and no later delivery is guaranteed to repair the lost evidence.
- **A value or identifier the write depends on, read from a row no fence of this batch gates.** Not only keys: a SET-clause subquery counts. Binding a caller-supplied `task_id`/`queue` into the target key rather than reading it off the stamped row (`f.task_id`, `f.queue`), fanning out over `waits.task_id` rather than over the runs the batch woke, or copying a deadline out of whatever row happens to match. Rule 5 requires the fence to bind the full argument surface; reading the surface back off the winning row is that requirement met by construction. A fenced read of ANOTHER table this batch stamped is fine — what is banned is unfenced, not cross-table.
- **A stamp used as proof of authorship.** Successor identity, replay guards, "did I create this row" — a stamp proves CURRENT provenance and any later transition (a claim, for instance) overwrites it, so a discriminator built on it answers "no successor" about a successor that is running. These must ask about immutable ownership (`successorOwned` in `fragments.ts`, including the intended attempt).
- **A multi-statement write outside `FencedBatch`.** A `db.batch(...)` in a store with two or more row-writing statements, or a store method that hand-rolls the stamp it needs. This removes every check above at once, and it is how the losing-sweeper race and the hand-minted wait stamp shipped. The exception is a batch carrying its own structural fence in the same batch — see `admin.ts` below.
- **In `fenced-batch.ts` or `sql-tree.ts`: caller text spliced into a boolean position without parentheses** (`rawSql` parenthesizes every predicate and value fragment, and a diff that stops it doing so is this shape), or a new exemption from the fence/OR scanners (a new statement kind, a new `open`-style flag, a per-statement bypass). AND binds tighter than OR, so an unbracketed `a OR b` compiles to `a OR (b AND fence)` and every row matching `a` enters the selection unstamped — this is finding 39, the class inside its own mechanism.
- **An `openTail` whose `reason` restates what the statement does rather than naming the thing that actually fences it.** `openTail` is exempt from the positive-fence and top-level-OR checks, and its tree form `openTailTree` from the gate alone, which makes it the widest door in the primitive; the reason string is the only thing standing in the gap, and it is decidable from the diff whether it names a fence (a unique index, a lease token, another batch's stamp) or merely paraphrases the SELECT.

Allowed cases (do NOT flag these):

- **`openTail` reads fenced by something other than this batch's stamp,** where the reason says what fences them instead. `claim`'s `picked` is keyed on the LEASE token precisely so a same-token retry returns the ORIGINAL selection a PREVIOUS batch stamped (§3.4 rule 4, receipt semantics). `spawn`'s `receipt` reads a task another caller created, fenced by the unique `(queue, idempotency_key)` index, and its store predicate is a top-level `OR` (`(t.task_id = ? AND t.queue = ?) OR (? IS NOT NULL AND t.queue = ? AND t.idempotency_key = ? AND t.task_id <> ?)`), which is the textbook flag shape and is correct here. `awaitEvent`'s `hit` reads the `events` row the EMITTING batch wrote.
- **Counter bumps inside a compare-and-set.** `claim_gen + 1` in claim's compare-and-set (`claimCas` in `packages/core/src/statements/claim-receipt.ts`) and `relaunch_count + 1` in the sweep's reopen (`reopenLostLaunchCas` in `packages/core/src/statements/sweep.ts`) are idempotent in context: the CAS's own guard consumes the pre-state, so a replay matches nothing. The ban on `x = x + n` is a follow-on rule only, and `FencedBatch` already enforces exactly that split.
- **A CAS reading tables this batch never wrote.** `awaitEvent`'s `register` guards on `NOT EXISTS (… events …)` plus EXISTS probes over `runs` and `tasks`; `claim`'s candidate subselect joins `tasks`. Consulting pre-state is what a compare-and-set is for.
- **The ownership predicate in `fragments.ts`,** which contains no fence by design. `successorOwned(id, task, attempt)` requires all three immutable identity fields; dropping the attempt arm lets a historical run of the same task suppress the intended successor and commit a half-transition.
- **The conflict arm of `checkpointWrite` (`packages/core/src/statements/checkpoint.ts`), `excluded.owner_attempt >= checkpoints.owner_attempt`.** A last-writer-wins tiebreak in the conflict branch, never the fence; the fence is the node `f.fence_stamp = fenceValue(binds.fence)` in the feeding SELECT (rule 5 names the tiebreaker as a tiebreaker).
- **`narrow:` clauses that only shrink.** `state IN ${LIVE}`, `NOT ${successorOwned(…)}`, the park's `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tasks t … t.state IN ${LIVE})`, and `claim`'s `waits-timeout` narrow comparing `timeout_at_ms` against `fencedAt('runs', 'f.run_id = waits.run_id', b.fence('claim'))` — including the `f` alias inside it, which is bound by that subquery's own FROM, not by the generated selection.
- **A parenthesised `OR` from the shared fragments,** i.e. `cancelNotDue` and therefore `eligibleTask`, anywhere in any statement. It is bracketed, so it cannot widen anything. Likewise an `OR` inside a `derived()` `where:`: the generator brackets the correlation (`(${spec.where}) AND f.fence_stamp = …`), so `(a OR b) AND fence` still admits only stamped rows.
- **Post-state values in a `derived()` `where:`** — `f.state = 'running'` in claim's `task-book`, `f.queue = ? AND f.state = 'pending'` in emit's `wake-tasks` and `waits-gone`. The generator ANDs the fence unconditionally, so the post-state there is an index access path, not the proof.
- **Generated provenance on `derived()` updates.** `wake-tasks` selects from the runs `wake-runs` stamped, and the primitive generates both its stamp and instant from that source fence. A caller cannot hand a generated update a different provenance source.
- **`emitEvent`'s `wake-runs` as it stands** — hand-written WHERE, the uncorrelated `IN` driver kept for the query plan, `s.queue = runs.queue` looking redundant (it is redundant for any single row, which is exactly why it is load-bearing across two), and the `runs.wake_step IS NULL` arm that lets pre-migration parks be woken. Do not flag it for being hand-written, and do not propose deleting the redundancy or correlating the driver — both are pinned, by `emit-wake-one-witness` in `scripts/mutation-probe.py` and by the write query-plan pin.
- **Single-statement raw writes in the store:** `heartbeat`'s `UPDATE … RETURNING` (one statement cannot have a later statement acting without proof, and its guard already binds run, queue, token, state and task liveness) and `expireLeaseNow`. Also `driverHeartbeat`'s two-statement raw batch: observability only, nothing in the protocol reads `drivers`, and its DELETE derives its instant from the beat row it just wrote rather than from a second clock read.
- **Read-mode batches** — `sweep:scan`, `get-checkpoints`, `task-result`, `next-wake`, `migrate:version`, and the exported `SWEEP_SCAN_*` / `NEXT_WAKE_SQL` constants. Nothing writes, so no fence is owed.
- **`admin.ts`'s migration batches.** `migrate:bootstrap` and `migrate:v<N>` are raw multi-statement writes on purpose: each carries its own structural fence in the same batch — a plain `INSERT INTO meta … 'applied:vN'` whose primary-key violation on a concurrent or stale re-apply rolls the whole batch back, plus a version bump guarded on the previous value and a post-condition asserted after the loop. Migration authors write plain DDL and cannot forget the fence.

Report the finding as a claim about rows, not about text: name the batch label and statement name, the rows it can write without proof, and the concrete interleaving that produces them — a stale actor whose CAS lost, a duplicate delivery of the same request, an exact replay, a replay after the world moved on (the successor has since been claimed and re-stamped), or a corrupt row some other actor left. State the invariant (§3.4 rule 1, 2 or 8) and the user-visible consequence in one sentence, since every bug in this class is silent. Then name the mechanism, because a review bot is a detection net of last resort and never a rung on the prevention ladder: say which layer should structurally have caught this and why it could not, and give the rung-1 fix where one exists — route the statement through `derived()`, take the identifier off the stamped row, ask about ownership instead of the stamp — otherwise name the machine-checked addition the fix must carry (a mutation in `scripts/mutation-probe.py`, a case in `packages/store-libsql/test/generated-selection.test.ts`, a row shape in the generated wake-witness surface, or a checker in `packages/conformance/src/invariants.ts`). If the only available fix is "read this more carefully next time", say so explicitly and call it a mechanism gap. Note for the author that a confirmed finding here is a SEV under CLAUDE.md: it requires a red test, the fix, and a postmortem in the same PR.
